routes.description: Establish that the earliest recoverable traditions and independent attestations are better explained by a mortal Jewish teacher whose life and teachings were rapidly transformed through scriptural, epic, theological, and communal mythmaking.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by grounding Jesus in early independent tradition, explaining Pauline silence without positing an exclusively celestial Christ, defending external or interpersonal attestation, and showing that extensive Gospel invention remains compatible with an underlying historical person.

motionBridge.description: Connect the surviving early-source evidence to a first-century Jewish teacher whose subsequent mythologization does not erase his historical existence.

centralBridges.description: Establish an early tradition independent of Gospel literary invention that presents Jesus as a mortal Jewish teacher concerned with law and God's kingdom.
Explain Paul's sparse earthly biography through the purposes of his letters while identifying traditions or relationships that connect Paul to an earthly Jesus movement.
Defend Josephus's James reference and related early testimony as evidence independently anchoring Jesus and his followers in history.
Show how extensive literary and theological transformation can elevate and obscure a historical teacher without requiring that the earthly figure was invented.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for variations in kingdom, Torah, and mission traditions through changing communities and social identities.
Show that shared historical tradition explains the relevant overlaps and developments without unnecessary dependence on wholesale literary reification.

routes.description: Establish that the earliest evidence is more expected if Christianity began with a revelatory Christ and that later authors placed this figure into an earthly story through scriptural and literary reification unsupported by secure independent corroboration.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by showing that Paul lacks expected traces of a recent earthly teacher, supplying a coherent revelatory and celestial origin model, explaining Gospel biography as later literary construction, and defeating purported independent attestations or demonstrations that the evidence discriminates in favor of historicity.

motionBridge.description: Connect the evidentiary pattern of early revelation and later historicization to the proposition that Christianity began without a recent earthly founder.

centralBridges.description: Show that Paul's repeated reliance on revelation and scripture, together with missing expected earthly references, differentially supports a revelatory-Christ origin.
Provide a historically coherent account in which an incarnate Christ is killed by supernatural powers and known to apostles through revelation.
Explain earthly Gospel narratives as literary transformations of Pauline, scriptural, communal, or revelatory materials rather than memories of a teacher.
Show that Josephus, kinship language, eyewitness claims, and later Christian texts do not securely provide independent attestation of a historical Jesus.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require contextual evidence that distinguishes historical-memory explanations from revelatory or literary-reification alternatives.
Constrain reconstruction according to the chronology, dependence, ambiguity, and scarcity of the surviving sources.

sections.title: Paul, revelation, and traces of an earthly life
sections.rationale: Paul is the earliest major evidence in dispute, and the competing explanations of his biographical omissions, revealed knowledge, teachings, and personal contacts directly distinguish the two origin models.

sections.title: Q, Jewish teaching, and kingdom traditions
sections.rationale: The status and independence of traditions about Torah reform, mission, apocalypse, and God's kingdom determine whether an early mortal teacher is recoverable before later Gospel composition.

sections.title: Gospel mythmaking and literary reification
sections.rationale: Both routes must explain how earthly narratives arose, including whether epic and scriptural transformation presupposes a historical subject or can manufacture one from prior revelatory and communal material.

sections.title: Josephus, James, and independent attestation
sections.rationale: The identification of James, the meaning and transmission of the kinship wording, and the legal context determine whether the debate has significant external evidence for Jesus.

sections.title: Later testimony, alternative Christians, and evidential method
sections.rationale: Johannine, Papian, Ignatian, Petrine, and Acts traditions test competing claims about eyewitness memory and early dissent, while comparative standards govern what these sparse sources can establish.
